analysis.one_liner: Requires big electric utilities to get a quarter of their power from renewables and steadily cut energy waste through 2040.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to a House committee and its energy subcommittee, never got a hearing or vote, and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act to create a national renewable electricity standard: large retail electric suppliers would have to submit federal renewable energy credits equal to at least 6% of their electricity sales in 2015, rising to 25% from 2025 through 2040 [S2][S3]. It would also set an energy efficiency resource standard, requiring large electricity and natural gas suppliers to achieve cumulative savings rising to 15% of electricity and 10% of natural gas by 2025, with states allowed to run the programs [S2][S3]. Suppliers could trade credits, buy savings from third parties, or pay alternative compliance fees that states would have to spend on renewables and efficiency [S2][S3]. The bill was introduced by Rep. Peter Welch in July 2014 with one cosponsor, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and sent to its Energy and Power Subcommittee; no hearing or vote ever followed [S4][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses that would save on energy bills through mandated efficiency, cleaner air from reduced fossil generation, and the renewable energy industry that would sell into a new national credit market [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Sets a rising national renewable electricity requirement, from 6% of sales in 2015 to 25% from 2025 through 2040, for large retail electric suppliers [S2][S3].

Requires large electricity and natural gas suppliers to achieve cumulative efficiency savings of 15% and 10% respectively by 2025, with a floor preventing standards from falling below 2025 levels [S2][S3].

Encourages state regulators to let utilities recover efficiency program costs, lost fixed-cost revenue, and shareholder incentives, designed so the standards do not fall on utility balance sheets alone [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal- and oil-fired generators and any utility slow to shift to renewables or efficiency, which face compliance costs or civil penalties; ratepayers may see some of those costs passed through in bills [S3].

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for utilities that fall short would be passed to customers in electricity and gas bills, and regions with less wind or sun could pay more, cushioned by a $50-per-megawatt-hour alternative compliance payment [S3].

The bill credits some biomass combustion as renewable, conditioned on a 50% lifecycle greenhouse-gas reduction versus an efficient gas plant, and relies on EPA guidelines for the carbon accounting — an approach critics of biomass-to-energy dispute [S3].
A national standard overlaps with rules 30 states and D.C. already had in place, and the federal floor could preempt stronger state programs unless states add requirements on top [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs a federal renewable mandate with an efficiency mandate that, by its own findings, targets savings that cost less than generating more power, and it includes rate-recovery and shareholder-incentive language to soften utility opposition. The honest cost is upfront compliance spending that shows up in bills before the savings do, and the biomass carve-outs that a careful carbon accounting would question. On the whole it is a sizable, cost-bounded push toward cheaper-to-consumers clean energy, not a giveaway.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Energy and Power Subcommittee from August 2014 until the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Peter Welch introduced the bill on July 30, 2014, for himself and Rep. Ben Ray Lujan of New Mexico [S3][S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S5].
On August 1, 2014, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power, and no further action was taken before the Congress ended [S5].
The bill's only listed cosponsors were the two Democratic sponsors themselves: one Democrat besides Welch appears in the record, Rep. Ben Ray Lujan, and no Republicans signed on [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Utilities, coal- and oil-fired generators, and natural gas suppliers avoided new federal renewable and efficiency mandates for the rest of the 113th Congress; renewable and efficiency companies lost the national market the bill would have created.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; both sponsors were Democrats and no Republicans cosponsored, so partisan shape can only be inferred from the absence of Republican support [S4].

industries.note: A rising 25% renewable requirement and efficiency mandates would shrink the market for their power and force investments or compliance payments; passing those costs to ratepayers would raise bills in the short run while efficiency savings offset them over time.

They face federal compliance duties and civil penalties for shortfalls, but the bill lets them trade credits, buy savings from third parties, and urges state regulators to let them recover efficiency costs and earn shareholder incentives if targets are met.
Large gas suppliers would face cumulative savings targets of up to 10% of deliveries by 2025 and penalties of $10 per million Btu for shortfalls, reducing the volume of gas they sell.

industries.industry: Renewable energy generators (wind, solar, hydro, geothermal, biomass)
industries.note: The bill creates a national market for federal renewable electricity credits they could sell to utilities, with multipliers for rooftop, Indian land, and brownfield projects.

industries.industry: Energy efficiency providers and energy service companies
industries.note: Utilities may buy verified savings from third-party efficiency providers to meet the standard, creating a new customer base for efficiency services.
